facts.claim: In the Armenian Apostolic marriage service, the right hands of the bride and groom are joined during the exchange of vows, as a sign of the couple's oneness.
facts.conflicts: Parish page of St. Sarkis Armenian Apostolic Church (US parish), not the Mother See; read live 2026-11-03.

facts.claim: The priest blesses the rings, which the bride and groom then exchange.

The rite of crowning is the high point of the Armenian Church wedding service; the crowns stand for the glory and honour with which God crowns the couple, who are crowned as king and queen of their own home.
A cup of wine is blessed in memory of the wedding at Cana, and the couple drink from this common cup as a sign that they will share everything in life, joys and sorrows.
The service closes with a benediction in which the priest asks Christ to protect the couple under the shadow of His cross.
facts.conflicts: The priest's blessing under the cross is sourced; the kavor physically holding a cross over the couple is NOT stated on this page.

facts.claim: One Armenian Apostolic parish's rules (St. Sarkis, US): the sacrament must follow the canons of the Armenian Apostolic Church and may not be held outside the church; a partner from a Protestant denomination must be confirmed in the Armenian Church; the best man must be a member of the Armenian Church; the couple must complete the pastor's pre-marital preparation.
facts.conflicts: Parish-level rules; the Diocese of Australia and New Zealand's rules were not found online in this run. Present as 'for example, one parish asks...' or as a booking-checklist item.

facts.claim: Holy Matrimony in the Armenian Church is described as the sacrament by which two baptised Christians enter a lifelong union by making vows before God and the Church.
facts.conflicts: Parish page of St. James Armenian Church, Watertown MA (US).

facts.claim: One Armenian parish (St. James, Watertown, US) does not hold weddings on Sunday mornings, during Great Lent or Holy Week, or on five major feasts: Armenian Christmas, Easter, the Transfiguration, the Assumption of the Holy Mother of God and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.
facts.conflicts: Parish rule; Australian diocese calendar not checked. Treat as 'ask your parish priest' guidance.

facts.claim: The same parish asks couples to contact it at least eight months before the wedding and to confirm the priest and church before booking anything else, with at least one pre-marital meeting with the pastor.
facts.conflicts: US parish lead time; not a general rule.

facts.claim: Smithsonian Folklife Festival (2018) staged a recreation of a traditional Armenian wedding, which it calls a harsanig, performed by a couple who had married in Armenia the year before; the programme's curator, Levon Abrahamian, noted that each region of Armenia has its own wedding style, though much of the symbolism is shared.
facts.conflicts: Smithsonian Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage blog, Micaela Nerguizian, 8 August 2018. Museum source. Supports the 'varies by region' framing line.

facts.claim: In that recreation, the zurna (a woodwind) and the kopal (a large double-headed drum) played, and guests danced folk dances around the couple, including the shabash, when guests throw money for the couple that is then swept up and given to the musicians, and the yarkhushta, a men's clap dance performed in facing pairs.
facts.conflicts: Overlaps batch B (music and dance). Not a UNESCO source; do not link to duduk or Kochari.

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account says the mother-in-law places lavash on the shoulders of the bride and groom as a sign of prosperity and abundance.
facts.conflicts: Overlaps batch B (lavash); batch B should use UNESCO wording for the inscription itself.

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account says the couple break plates before entering their new home to cast off evil, and that by tradition whoever breaks a plate first takes charge of the household.
facts.conflicts: Overlaps batch B (plate). Present the 'who is in charge' line lightly, as tradition says.

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account says that as the couple enter the groom's house, the mother-in-law gives them a spoonful of honey and walnuts, wishing them a sweet life.
facts.conflicts: Overlaps batch B (welcome at the groom's home).

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account describes the tzaghkatz khndzor ('flourished apple'): a groomsman holds a knife or sword topped with an apple set with coins (traditionally gold and silver), the blade draped in red and green ribbon, red for the bride and green for the groom, with sweets for a sweet start.
facts.conflicts: Spelling as given by the source. Red/green ribbon meaning is sourced only here; do not extend to the old page's red dress and crown claims.

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account says toasts are central: both the godfather and the mother-in-law speak in praise of the couple, followed by poetry and song.
facts.conflicts: Sources a 'godfather' role at the celebration only; the kavor's church role remains [[VERIFY]].

facts.claim: The Smithsonian account says the bride's family presents handmade items to the groom's family, such as a bedcover, tablecloth, baby blanket and a silk rug, as signs of the bride's patience and skill.
facts.conflicts: Historic custom shown at a recreation; frame as tradition, not current expectation. No amounts.

facts.claim: UNESCO element title, exact: 'Lavash, the preparation, meaning and appearance of traditional bread as an expression of culture in Armenia'. Inscribed in 2014 (9.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

UNESCO's lavash text says lavash 'plays a ritual role in weddings, where it is placed on the shoulders of newlyweds to bring fertility and prosperity'. (UNESCO wording; paraphrase as UNESCO describes it, e.g. 'laid on the newlyweds' shoulders as a wish for fertility and prosperity'.)

UNESCO's lavash text: preparation is typically done by a small group of women; the dough of wheat flour and water is rolled thin, stretched over an oval cushion and slapped against the wall of a traditional conical clay oven; the group baking strengthens family, community and social ties.
UNESCO element title, exact: 'Duduk and its music'. Inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List, originally proclaimed in 2005.

UNESCO's duduk text says duduk music 'accompanies popular Armenian traditional songs and dances of the various regions and is played at events, such as weddings and funerals'. It is usually played by two musicians, one holding a continuous drone by circular breathing while the other plays the melody.

UNESCO's duduk text: the body is ideally made from apricot wood; there are four major types, 28 to 40 cm long; the 40 cm duduk is regarded as most suited to love songs, the smaller one usually accompanies dances. UNESCO also notes it is played less in popular festivities and more as staged performance by professionals.
UNESCO element title, exact: 'Kochari, traditional group dance'. Inscribed in 2017 (12.COM) on the Representative List. Correct URL ends 01295 (the 01291 URL resolves to Greece's Rebetiko).

UNESCO's Kochari text says it is 'widely performed throughout Armenia during holidays, festive celebrations, family ceremonies and other social events' and is 'open to all participants, irrespective of age, gender or social status'. UNESCO's description text does not say 'wedding' in the body (the page's keyword tags include 'Wedding'); it does not describe how dancers hold hands or shoulders.

Smartraveller CNI page (last updated 1 October 2026): if you're getting married overseas, local authorities may ask you to prove you aren't already married; a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued to support an intended marriage overseas. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail. At least one applicant must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident.

Smartraveller CNI page: DFAT can't advise on another country's legal processes; couples should ask the destination's embassy in Australia or the local authority responsible for marriage whether a CNI is needed (a Single Status Certificate or No Record Result Certificate from a state or territory registry may be accepted instead), whether it must be issued in that country, and whether it needs an apostille or authentication.

Smartraveller CNI page: the local authority may ask for other documents, such as a birth certificate or a divorce certificate; ask whether these need legalising. DFAT charges fees for CNIs (fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year). No amount is recorded here, per the brief.

insider_details.detail: Book the parish before anything else: one Armenian Apostolic parish asks for at least eight months' notice and wants the priest and church confirmed before any other wedding booking, so lock the church date first and build the reception and travel around it.

Check the church calendar before choosing a date: at least one parish will not marry couples during Great Lent, Holy Week, on Sunday mornings or on five major feast days, so a spring date near Easter needs the priest's sign-off before guests book flights.

Plan the church running sheet around the crowning, the high point of the service, and the shared cup straight after it; brief the photographer to capture both from below the altar steps, as parishes can restrict where photographers stand.

If one partner is not Armenian Apostolic, raise it with the parish priest early: one parish requires a Protestant partner to be confirmed in the Armenian Church and the best man (the church sponsor) to be a church member, and pre-marital preparation with the pastor is expected.

Ask the band early whether they will play for the shabash, when guests throw money that goes to the musicians, and agree with the venue on a clean-up moment, plus a safe, open floor area if the men plan a yarkhushta.

The threshold rituals (lavash on the shoulders, honey and walnuts, a plate broken at the door) happen at the groom's home or new home, so for a destination wedding agree with the venue where the 'door' moment will be staged and who plays the mother-in-law's role.

If you want lavash on your shoulders as a guest-facing moment, plan it at the arrival at the reception or the family home and brief the photographer; UNESCO ties lavash to weddings in exactly this way, so it reads as heritage rather than a gimmick.

UNESCO describes the duduk as usually played by two musicians (a drone and a melody), so book a pair rather than a soloist if you want the traditional sound, and allow for the longer duduk for a slow, romantic piece.
Kochari is open to every age and is danced at family ceremonies, so it works as the moment that gets both grandparents and friends onto the floor; plan floor space for a large group line.

Australia has no mission in Armenia and DFAT says some authorities accept only a CNI issued in-country, so ask the Armenian registry early whether an Australian-issued CNI (or a state registry single status certificate) is accepted, and whether it needs an apostille, before anyone books flights.

For Armenian-Australian couples, remind any dual-national groom and family that Smartraveller says dual nationals must travel on the Armenian passport, and that male dual nationals aged 18 to 28 may be liable for military service; raise it at the first planning call, not at check-in.
Keep wedding events, coach transfers and day trips well away from the 5 km band along the Azerbaijan border that Smartraveller rates Level 4; Yerevan-based plans keep logistics simple.
